---
title: "The Economist chart style guide: 2024 onward"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
## Fold each chunk's code behind a "Code" toggle; output stays visible.
local({
  source_hook <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("source")
  knitr::knit_hooks$set(source = function(x, options) {
    paste0("\n\n<details><summary>Code</summary>\n\n", source_hook(x, options), "\n\n</details>\n\n")
  })
})
```

```{css, echo = FALSE}
/* pkgdown gives every table Bootstrap's `table` class, whose cells are filled with --bs-table-bg (white); let the
   gt tables show their own background instead. */
table.gt_table { --bs-table-bg: transparent; }
```

*The Economist* redesigned its charts in March 2024, and has published no chart style guide since.
This article is a reverse-engineered replacement for *The Economist visual styleguide* (v1.2, 4 May 2017), which [another article](economist-2017-styleguide.html) reproduces.
Like the [classic guide](economist-classic-styleguide.html), it follows the sections of the 2017 guide and draws the 2017 guide's own example charts, with the same data, titles and sizes, in the new style, so that each figure here can be set beside its 2017 version.
It is not an official Economist specification.

The figures are *ggplot2* drawings made with `theme_economist_2024()`, `economist_2024_pal()` and the other 2024 tools in ggthemes.
The rules come from the charts themselves:

1. the public [Economist Design System](https://design-system.economist.com/) and [Marber color foundations](https://marber.economist.com/8e1dcf0b8/p/543b0f-colour/b/37fc5e);
2. charts published after the redesign in the local `econ-chart-corpus`: 94 print charts (April 2024 to August 2026, 29 of them from one 2026 issue) and about 420 web graphics (April 2024 to August 2026), whose responsive `ai2html` files carry their text styles; and
3. recurring conventions in [Graphic Detail](https://www.economist.com/topics/graphic-detail) and the [weekly edition](https://www.economist.com/weeklyedition).

Corpus charts are cited by their codes, such as `20240406_BRC149`: the issue date and the chart's name in the paper's system.
Exact colors are sampled values; layout rules are repeated observations, with counts where the corpus has enough charts to count.
After each chart, "Against 2017" says what changed, with a link to the 2017 version.
Where a 2017 chart type no longer appears in the corpus, the chart is drawn anyway, for comparison, and the text says so.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
## The 2024 palettes, the theme at the guide's size and the drawing helpers, shared with the child documents.
source("economist-2024-guide.R")
```

## What changed in 2024

The redesign replaced the cool blue print ground and blue-first palettes with a warm gray print ground and red-first palettes.
Web charts remain white, but share the red-led hierarchy; a white ground does not by itself mean a web graphic (see [A white ground with a short red tab](#a-white-ground-with-a-short-red-tab)).
The local corpus last shows the old cool ground on 16 March 2024 and first shows `#ECEBE0` on 30 March; the weekly indicator tables changed between the issues of 6 January and 6 April.
The charts changed with the paper's typeface, which it explained in ["Why has *The Economist* changed its typeface?"](https://www.economist.com/the-economist-explains/2024/02/07/why-has-the-economist-changed-its-typeface) (7 February 2024).

| Element | 2017 system | 2024 onward |
|---|---|---|
| Print ground | cool pale blue `#E7F0F5` | warm gray `#ECEBE0` |
| Web ground | white | white |
| First categorical color | blue | red |
| Supporting categories | blue, cyan, gold, teal | salmon, blue, light blue, dark gray, light gray |
| Text | black and blue-gray | near-black, with a gray source |
| Type | Econ Sans Condensed, 9.5pt headline | Economist Sans, a larger headline and subtitle |
| Top furniture | red tab; a full red rule on the web | a short red tab only |
| Panel headings | a short red marker | a short black rule |
| Number box | filled | outlined in black |
| Pie / doughnut | included | no longer used (none in 88 print or 118 web charts) |

The range of charts widened too. Every 2017 chart type is still drawn, but print now also carries more statistical forms: confidence ribbons on lines (`20250329_EPC233`), rank charts (`20240720_CNC447`), scatters with highlighted dots over a faded background (`20240706_ASC302`, `20240601_BRC147`), a scatter over time with a forecast band (`20250906_WBC303`), log scales on a lollipop (`20240608_WBC240`) and a scatter, forecasts drawn as dotted lines (`20240720_BRC433`), a stacked area with a total line and an unstacked line (`20250201_USC522`), a line chart with only event rules (`20240727_AMC511`), lines in an ordered color ramp (`20240420_EPC345`), and tables whose figures sit in colored boxes (`20241214_USC174`).
The sections below describe each. Counts of "rare" types in this guide come from its sample (see [Method and limitations](#method-and-limitations)), so a type that is rare there may be less rare in the full print archive.

What did not change is as important: the value axis on the right with its labels above the gridlines, the black baseline with ticks hanging below it, truncated years, unboxed panels, a left-aligned headline over a subtitle that gives the measure and unit, and a source line at the foot.

## Chart sizes

The 2017 guide prescribed named print modules, in points.
Current production is better understood as two separate compositions:

- **Print:** the entire graphic, headline and source included, sits on warm gray `#ECEBE0`.
  The corpus often contains 608px-wide delivery images; that is an asset size, not a physical width.
- **Web:** the entire graphic is white. Every `ai2html` graphic in the corpus has three artboards, at 700px, 550px and (for mobile) about 336px.
  Labels and panels reflow at the breakpoints; the desktop chart is not merely shrunk.
- **Alignment:** tab, headline, subtitle, plot and source share one left edge.

The figures here keep the 2017 guide's sizes (`economist_2017_size()`), and the 2017 guide's 7pt axis labels (`base_size = 7`), so each can be set beside its 2017 version at the same size.
`theme_economist_2024()` sets every other size as a multiple of `base_size`.

## Typefaces

Standard charts use Economist Sans, which replaced the condensed Econ Sans of 2017 when the paper changed its typeface in early 2024 ([explainer](https://www.economist.com/the-economist-explains/2024/02/07/why-has-the-economist-changed-its-typeface)).
It is not public: `economist_2017_font()` picks the closest installed substitute, Fira Sans Condensed, then Roboto Condensed, then `"sans"`.
The axis labels and the source are set in a light weight, which a theme cannot ask for; pass a light family as `base_family` to match them.

Footnotes are marked in the same order as in 2017.

```{r g24-footnote-symbols}
economist_2017_footnote(1:8)
```

```{r g24-footnote-figure, econ_size = "two_column", econ_height = 75}
## The label on the left over a rule, the eight symbols on the right, in the 2024 source gray.
g24_symbols <- data.frame(x = 0.36 + 0.08 * (0:7), number = 1:8, symbol = economist_2017_footnote(1:8))
g24_gray <- econ$print$source

g24_footnotes <- ggplot(g24_symbols, aes(x, 0)) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 1, y = 1.15, yend = 1.15, colour = g24_gray, linewidth = 0.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.55, label = "Footnote symbols", hjust = 0, vjust = 1, fontface = "bold",
           colour = g24_gray, size = g24_pt(7.5)) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.05, label = "order of use", hjust = 0, vjust = 1, colour = g24_gray,
           size = g24_pt(7.5)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = number), size = g24_pt(7), hjust = 1, vjust = 0, nudge_y = 0.05, colour = g24_gray) +
  geom_text(aes(x = x + 0.006, label = symbol), size = g24_pt(14), hjust = 0, vjust = 0.5, nudge_y = -0.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1.8), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  g24_theme() +
  g24_no_axes()

g24_chart(g24_footnotes)
```

## Anatomy of a chart

A standard chart reads from top to bottom:

1. a short red tab on the top edge: in print about 3.4 times the axis-label size wide and 0.45 high, inset with the chart; on the web about 2.7 by 0.27, flush left;
2. a bold, sentence-case headline;
3. a subtitle giving geography, measure, unit and period, bold in print and medium on the web;
4. a key or panel heading, when needed;
5. the plot;
6. notes and source below the baseline.

The value axis sits on the right, with each label just above its gridline at the right-hand end, as in 2017 (`20240330_CNC083`, `20240406_BRC149`): `scale_y_continuous(position = "right")` with `guide_axis_economist_2017()` produces it.
The baseline is black, with ticks hanging below it; the gridlines are pale and there is no panel box.

```{r g24-anatomy-bare, econ_height = 165}
## Monthly yields, in years since the start: the 2017 guide's data.
tokyo_x <- c(1, seq(1.25, 13.5, by = 0.25), 13.7)
g24_bonds <- data.frame(
  year = rep(tokyo_x, 2),
  yield = c(
    4.7, 5.0, 5.2, 5.1, 5.6, 6.6, 6.7, 7.9, 6.8, 6.5, 6.7, 6.2, 5.7, 5.5, 5.4, 4.9, 4.6, 4.2, 4.5, 4.0,
    3.4, 3.9, 4.1, 4.5, 4.5, 3.9, 3.0, 3.0, 2.9, 3.2, 3.2, 2.9, 2.5, 2.5, 2.6, 2.1, 1.9, 1.8, 1.6, 1.1,
    1.5, 1.8, 1.6, 1.8, 1.8, 1.8, 1.7, 1.9, 1.6, 1.2, 1.2, 1.25,
    4.7, 5.2, 5.8, 5.9, 6.3, 6.2, 6.2, 5.8, 5.4, 5.0, 5.3, 4.7, 4.9, 5.2, 4.8, 4.0, 4.0, 3.8, 3.6, 4.3,
    4.2, 4.2, 4.6, 4.1, 4.2, 4.4, 4.1, 4.3, 4.4, 4.8, 5.1, 4.7, 4.6, 4.6, 5.0, 4.5, 4.0, 3.6, 4.0, 3.7,
    2.7, 2.8, 3.6, 3.4, 3.6, 3.7, 3.2, 2.6, 3.1, 3.4, 3.0, 2.3
  ),
  period = rep(c("January 1989 (Japan)", "January 1999 (US)"), each = length(tokyo_x))
)

g24_tokyo <- ggplot(g24_bonds, aes(year, yield, colour = period)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = g24_lw(1.5)) +
  g24_value_axis(limits = c(0, 8), breaks = seq(0, 8, 2), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(1, 13.7), breaks = 1:13, labels = ifelse(1:13 %in% c(1, 5, 10, 13), 1:13, ""), expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_colour_economist_2024("print") +
  labs(
    title = "Where Tokyo leads",
    subtitle = "Ten-year government-bond yields, %",
    x = "Years since start", y = NULL, colour = "Period beginning:"
  ) +
  g24_theme()

g24_tokyo
```

The theme sets the 2024 type and rules: a headline 1.33 times the axis labels, a subtitle 1.13 times, pale gridlines, a black baseline with outward ticks, keys flush left above the plot, and a source as large as the axis labels, in gray.
As in 2017, three features are not theme elements:

* the **red tab** on the top edge;
* the **short black rule** over each panel heading;
* the **number box**, a square outlined in black at the top right.

`economist_2024_chart()` adds them to a finished plot and returns a grob you can print or save.

```{r g24-anatomy-chart, econ_height = 165}
g24_chart(g24_tokyo + labs(caption = "Source: Thomson Reuters"))
```

Against 2017: the ground is warm gray, the first line red and the second salmon, where 2017 drew them in blue and cyan; the headline and subtitle are larger, and the source is as large as the axis labels. `r g24_2017("anatomy-of-a-chart")`

## Source, footnote and number box

Put a note either on its own line above the source (28 of the 43 print charts with notes) or ranged right on the source line (15).
A numbered box appears only when the chart belongs to a numbered sequence: 34 of 88 print charts have one, a small square outlined in black at the top right, level with the headline, where 2017 filled it.

```{r g24-anatomy-print, econ_height = 165}
fn <- economist_2017_footnote(1:2)

g24_chart(
  g24_tokyo +
    labs(
      subtitle = paste0("Ten-year government-bond yields", fn[1], ", %"),
      ## The commoner 2024 layout: the note on its own line above the source.
      caption = paste0(fn[1], "Annualised\nSource: Thomson Reuters")
    ),
  number = 1
)
```

The web chart is white, and since 2024 it has no red rule across its top: the short tab is the only red furniture, and the key stays under the subtitle rather than moving up beside the headline.

```{r g24-anatomy-web, econ_size = "two_column", econ_height = 190}
## Olympic medal sweeps; the 1996 games had none.
g24_sweeps <- data.frame(
  year = c(1948, 1952, 1956, 1960, 1964, 1968, 1972, 1976, 1980, 1984, 1988, 1992, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016),
  us = c(5, 6, 6, 4, 4, 6, 2, 4, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 2, 3, 0, 1),
  ussr = c(0, 4, 1, 4, 0, 0, 2, 3, 5, 0, 3, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0),
  eg = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 6, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0),
  other = c(2, 0, 3, 0, 0, 1, 4, 2, 0, 0, 3, 3, 2, 2, 4, 2, 0)
)
g24_sweeps <- data.frame(
  year = rep(g24_sweeps$year, 4),
  count = c(g24_sweeps$other, g24_sweeps$eg, g24_sweeps$ussr, g24_sweeps$us),
  country = factor(
    rep(c("Other", "East Germany", "Soviet Union", "United States"), each = nrow(g24_sweeps)),
    levels = c("United States", "Soviet Union", "East Germany", "Other")
  )
)

g24_anthem <- ggplot(g24_sweeps, aes(year, count, fill = country)) +
  geom_col(width = 2.7, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  annotate("text", x = 1992, y = 1.55, label = "*", colour = "white", size = g24_text) +
  ## Red, salmon and blue for the three countries, light gray for "Other".
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "United States" = w24[["red"]], "Soviet Union" = w24[["salmon"]],
      "East Germany" = w24[["blue"]], "Other" = w24[["light gray"]]
    )
  ) +
  g24_value_axis(limits = c(0, 12), breaks = seq(0, 12, 2), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1948, 2016, 4), labels = economist_2017_year_format(), expand = c(0.01, 0)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "National anthem monopolies", subtitle = "Number of “medal sweeps” by country",
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL,
    caption = "*Unified team of ex-Soviet republics\nSources: International Olympic Committee; Sports Reference; The Economist"
  ) +
  g24_theme("web")

g24_chart(g24_anthem, "web")
```

Against 2017: no red rule, the key under the subtitle in one row, and the note above the source rather than ranged right on its line. `r g24_2017("source-footnote-and-number-box")`

## Type scale and margins

Across the 700px `ai2html` files the type scale is fixed: 20px/24px bold headlines (62 of 63 charts), 17px/20px medium subtitles (46 of 63), 15px light axis numbers and 15px/20px light source text in gray `#666666` (62 of 63).
Print charts set the subtitle bolder than the web does.
`theme_economist_2024()` takes `base_size` as the axis-label size and sets the rest as multiples of it:

| Role | Treatment | Multiple of axis-label size | At `base_size = 7` | Theme element |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| Headline | bold, black | 20/15 = 1.33 | 9.3pt | `plot.title` |
| Subtitle | medium on the web, bold in print | 17/15 = 1.13 | 7.9pt | `plot.subtitle` |
| Panel heading | bold, under a short black rule | 1.13 | 7.9pt | `strip.text` |
| Axes, keys, annotation | light, black | 1 | 7pt | `axis.text`, `legend.text` |
| Source and notes | light, gray | 1 | 7pt | `plot.caption` |

The source is as large as the axis labels, and the axis labels are black, not gray.
A print chart has a small outer inset; a web chart has none.
Keep at least one line of clear space between the subtitle or key and the marks.

### Leader block

Charts in the Leaders section drop the tab and set the headline in red, as a single line naming the measure that also does the subtitle's work.

```{r g24-leader, econ_size = "leader"}
## Monthly, January 2011 to mid-2015.
g24_leader_data <- data.frame(
  year = c(2011.02, 2011 + (1:55) / 12),
  change = c(
    1.47, 1.56, 1.85, 2.19, 2.58, 2.69, 2.72, 2.81, 2.88, 2.84, 2.73, 2.61, 2.54, 2.54, 2.45, 2.19,
    1.85, 1.62, 1.52, 1.49, 1.63, 1.82, 1.82, 1.67, 1.59, 1.61, 1.52, 1.25, 1.22, 1.42, 1.57, 1.51,
    1.31, 1.12, 1.13, 1.3, 1.4, 1.25, 1.24, 1.51, 1.71, 1.73, 1.7, 1.64, 1.53, 1.45, 1.28, 0.98,
    0.51, 0.21, 0.27, 0.22, 0.2, 0.29, 0.32, 0.33
  )
)
g24_leader <- ggplot(g24_leader_data, aes(year, change)) +
  geom_line(colour = single24[["print"]], linewidth = g24_lw(1.2)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 2, colour = "black", linewidth = g24_lw(0.5)) +
  annotate("text", x = 2015.95, y = 2.08, label = "Fed target  2", hjust = 1, vjust = 0, size = g24_pt(6)) +
  g24_value_axis(limits = c(0, 3), breaks = c(0, 1, 3), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(2011, 2016), breaks = c(2011:2015, 2015.57), labels = c(economist_2017_year(2011:2015), ""),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  labs(title = "US consumer prices,\n% increase on a year earlier", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  g24_theme(base_size = 6) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(colour = accent24[["print"]]))

g24_chart(g24_leader, tab = c(0, 0))
```

Against 2017: no tab, and the headline is red and carries the measure; the line is the single-series red, and the target line is black rather than red, which is kept for the data. `r g24_2017("leader-block")`

### Espresso lead image

The corpus has no Espresso images, so the chart below applies the standard rules at the 2017 Espresso size.

```{r g24-espresso, econ_size = "espresso"}
g24_espresso_data <- data.frame(
  year = 2007:2015,
  change = c(4, 2, -5.7, 4.4, 6.8, 4.1, 2.9, 3, 0.9)
)
g24_espresso <- ggplot(g24_espresso_data, aes(year, change)) +
  geom_col(fill = single24[["print"]], width = 0.67) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "black", linewidth = g24_lw(0.5)) +
  g24_value_axis(limits = c(-8, 8), breaks = seq(-8, 8, 4), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2007:2015, labels = economist_2017_year_format()) +
  labs(
    title = "US retail sales",
    subtitle = "Excluding motor vehicles and parts,\n% change on a year earlier",
    x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = "Source: US Department of Commerce"
  ) +
  g24_theme(base_size = 6) +
  ## 120pt of chart, then 40pt blank, as in 2017.
  theme(plot.margin = margin(0, 6, 6 + 40, 6, "pt"))

g24_chart(g24_espresso)
```

Against 2017: single-series red columns from a black zero line, where 2017 drew blue columns from a red one. `r g24_2017("espresso-lead-image")`

### Panel chart

Panels are set side by side or stacked, each headed in bold under a short black rule the length of the tab.

```{r g24-panel, econ_size = "two_column", econ_height = 195}
## The "Racy" chart: daily lines on the left, 12 points on the right.
panel_names <- c(
  "Donald Trump’s media dominance\nand polling surge",
  "Support for Trump v racial resentment\nand authoritarianism†,\nRepublican primary voters"
)
tv_mentions <- c(
  34, 29, 26, 35, 47, 56, 58, 55, 61, 64, 59, 55, 52, 52, 55, 58, 62, 61, 61, 58, 52, 50, 48, 53, 47, 41,
  41, 43, 42, 43, 47, 47, 48, 45, 35, 27, 27, 27, 27, 28, 37, 48, 50, 49, 57, 67, 63, 53, 55, 58, 56, 56,
  57, 57, 54, 54, 58, 57, 54, 45, 35, 35, 43, 48, 49, 53, 60, 64, 60, 60, 62, 69, 71, 69, 72, 70, 67, 69,
  71, 71, 71, 68, 70
)
polling <- c(
  3.8, 3.8, 4.1, 5.2, 6.2, 6.4, 9.3, 13, 16.7, 18.1, 19.3, 21.6, 23.6, 23.7, 22.5, 22.2, 22, 22.5, 24.4,
  26.5, 27.6, 28.8, 29.9, 30.4, 28, 24.8, 23.4, 23, 23.1, 23.4, 23.4, 24.8, 26.7, 27, 26.9, 25.7, 24.8,
  24.8, 24.5, 24.4, 26.1, 27.8, 28.6, 29.5, 29.8, 30.2, 31.6, 33.8, 34.5, 36, 35.5, 34.9, 34.6, 34.5,
  34.5, 34.7, 34.7, 35.7, 35.6, 34, 30.8, 29.3, 31.1, 33.6, 33.4, 33.9, 35.3, 36.2, 36.2, 34.1, 34.8,
  39.4, 42.9, 42.3, 41.4, 40.2, 39.3, 39.7, 40.4, 40.7, 42.2, 43.6, 45.3
)
days <- (6 * seq_along(tv_mentions) - 22) / 1.57
g24_panel_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(panel = panel_names[1], x = days, series = "TV mentions", value = tv_mentions),
  ## The polling average has its own 0-50 axis, so it is drawn at twice its value.
  data.frame(panel = panel_names[1], x = days, series = "Polling average", value = 2 * polling),
  data.frame(
    panel = panel_names[2], x = 1:12, series = "Authoritarianism",
    value = c(43.5, 42.9, 42.6, 43.5, 44.4, 45.3, 46.4, 47.7, 48.9, 49.9, 50.4, 50.6)
  ),
  data.frame(
    panel = panel_names[2], x = 1:12, series = "Racial resentment",
    value = c(2, 9.5, 17.3, 24.9, 31.4, 35.3, 39.1, 43, 46.5, 50, 53.5, 56)
  )
)
g24_panel_data$panel <- factor(g24_panel_data$panel, levels = panel_names)

## The two lines of each panel: red and blue, so that each colored axis reads apart from the other.
g24_first <- p24[["red"]]
g24_second <- p24[["blue"]]
g24_note <- econ$print$source
g24_panel_plot <- function(panel_pt) {
  up1 <- 100 / panel_pt # data units of the first panel per point
  up2 <- 60 / panel_pt
  txt <- function(data, size = g24_size) {
    geom_text(
      data = data, aes(.data$x, .data$y, label = .data$label, hjust = .data$hjust), colour = data$colour,
      size = g24_pt(size), inherit.aes = FALSE
    )
  }
  lab <- function(panel, x, y, label, hjust = 0.5, colour = "black") {
    data.frame(panel = factor(panel_names[panel], levels = panel_names), x = x, y = y, label = label,
               hjust = hjust, colour = colour)
  }
  axis_labels <- rbind(
    lab(1, -49.6, seq(0, 100, 20) + 4 * up1, seq(0, 100, 20), hjust = 0, colour = g24_second),
    lab(1, 342, seq(0, 100, 20) + 4 * up1, seq(0, 50, 10), hjust = 1, colour = g24_first),
    lab(2, 13.7, seq(0, 60, 20) + 4 * up2, seq(0, 60, 20), hjust = 1)
  )
  unit_labels <- rbind(
    lab(1, -49.6, 100 + 13 * up1, "TV mentions*, % of total", hjust = 0, colour = g24_second),
    lab(1, 342, 100 + 13 * up1, "Polling average, %", hjust = 1, colour = g24_first),
    lab(2, 13.7, 60 + 13 * up2, "Voter support, %", hjust = 1)
  )
  months <- lab(
    1, c(-4.4, 15.3, 46, 76.3, 105.5, 135.4, 165, 195, 226, 255.5, 285, 307.6), -9.5 * up1,
    c("J", "J", "A", "S", "O", "N", "D", "J", "F", "M", "A", "M")
  )
  years <- lab(1, c(86, 243), -19 * up1, c("2015", "2016"))
  direct_labels <- lab(2, c(1.2, 6.8), c(50, 32.5), c("Authoritarianism", "Racial resentment"), hjust = 0)
  scale_labels <- rbind(
    lab(2, 0.33, -9 * up2, "LOWEST", hjust = 0, colour = g24_note),
    lab(2, 12, -9 * up2, "HIGHEST", colour = g24_note)
  )
  scale_text <- lab(
    2, 7, c(-4.5, -13.5) * up2, c("Degree of authoritarianism", "Level of resentment"), colour = g24_note
  )
  scale_arrow <- data.frame(
    panel = factor(panel_names[2], levels = panel_names), x = 3.6, xend = 10.2, y = -9 * up2
  )
  ggplot(g24_panel_data, aes(.data$x, .data$value, colour = .data$series)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = g24_lw(1.2), show.legend = FALSE) +
    txt(axis_labels) +
    txt(unit_labels) +
    txt(months) +
    txt(years) +
    txt(direct_labels) +
    txt(scale_labels, 6.5) +
    txt(scale_text, 6.5) +
    geom_segment(
      data = scale_arrow, aes(x = .data$x, xend = .data$xend, y = .data$y, yend = .data$y), colour = g24_note,
      linewidth = 0.3, arrow = grid::arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(3, "pt"), type = "closed"),
      inherit.aes = FALSE
    ) +
    facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
    coord_cartesian(clip = "off", expand = FALSE) +
    ## Set the panel ranges so the lettering outside the axes does not stretch them.
    scale_x_continuous(
      limits = function(limits) if (diff(limits) > 100) c(-49.6, 342) else c(0.326, 13.7), oob = scales::oob_keep,
      breaks = function(limits) {
        if (limits[2] > 100) c(-9, 0, 31, 62, 92, 123, 153, 184, 215, 244, 275, 305) else c(1, 12)
      },
      labels = function(breaks) rep("", length(breaks))
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      limits = function(limits) if (max(limits) > 80) c(0, 100) else c(0, 60), oob = scales::oob_keep,
      position = "right",
      breaks = function(limits) seq(0, limits[2], 20)
    ) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(
      "TV mentions" = g24_second, "Polling average" = g24_first,
      "Authoritarianism" = g24_second, "Racial resentment" = g24_first
    )) +
    labs(title = "Racy", subtitle = "United States", x = " ", y = NULL) +
    g24_theme() +
    theme(
      axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y.right = element_blank(),
      strip.text = element_text(margin = margin(3.5, 0, 18, 0))
    )
}

g24_chart(
  g24_panel_plot(60) +
    labs(caption = paste0(
      "*National news mentions of Trump compared with all Republican candidates\n",
      "†Poll Jul 30th-Aug 6th 2016\nSources: GDELT; RCP; YouGov"
    ))
)
```

Against 2017: each panel heading opens with a short black rule instead of a red marker; the lines are red and blue rather than red, teal and maroon, and the notes stand above the source. `r g24_2017("panel-chart")`

Portrait panel charts stack the panels in one column.

```{r g24-panel-portrait, econ_height = 350}
g24_chart(
  g24_panel_plot(68) +
    facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free", axes = "all") +
    labs(caption = paste0(
      "*National news mentions of\nTrump compared with all\nRepublican candidates\n",
      "†Poll Jul 30th-Aug 6th 2016\nSources: GDELT;\nRCP; YouGov"
    ))
)
```

## Color

Color is semantic. Red establishes focus; salmon is a related or less emphatic category; blue and light blue form the main contrast; grays provide context.
Do not use the whole palette merely because six colors are available. Ordered categories take a ramp instead (see [Ordered categories](#ordered-categories)).

The palettes here are provisional. They are measured from the charts the corpus happens to hold: the web set is well attested, but the print set rests largely on one chart, and the ramps are reconstructions.
They will be updated when a better corpus of examples is available.

```{r g24-swatches, econ_size = "two_column", econ_height = 230}
## The palettes, grouped as the 2017 guide groups its swatches.
g24_swatch_rows <- list(
  list("PRINT", p24),
  list("WEB", w24),
  list("REDS", c(
    "print emphasis" = accent24[["print"]], "print single" = single24[["print"]],
    "web emphasis" = accent24[["web"]], "web single" = single24[["web"]]
  )),
  list("BACKGROUND", c(
    "print ground" = econ$print$bg$value[1], "print panel alt" = econ$print$bg$value[2],
    "web ground" = econ$web$bg$value[1]
  )),
  list("NEUTRAL", c(
    "print grid" = econ$print$grid, "print text" = econ$print$text, "print source" = econ$print$source,
    "web grid" = econ$web$grid, "web text" = econ$web$text, "web source" = econ$web$source
  ))
)
g24_swatch_data <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(g24_swatch_rows), function(r) {
  hex <- g24_swatch_rows[[r]][[2]]
  data.frame(group = g24_swatch_rows[[r]][[1]], row = r, col = seq_along(hex), name = toupper(names(hex)), hex = hex)
}))

ggplot(g24_swatch_data, aes(col, -row)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = hex), width = 0.94, height = 0.42, colour = econ$web$grid, linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_text(aes(y = -row + 0.36, label = name), size = g24_pt(4), vjust = 0) +
  geom_text(aes(y = -row - 0.32, label = hex), size = g24_pt(4), vjust = 1) +
  geom_text(
    data = unique(g24_swatch_data[c("group", "row")]), aes(x = -1.2, y = -row, label = group),
    size = g24_pt(6), fontface = "bold", hjust = 0, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1.2, 6.6), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(title = "Chart palette, print and web", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  g24_theme("web") +
  g24_no_axes()
```

Against 2017: one order for every chart type, where the 2017 guide set a different order for bars, stacked bars, lines, dots and pies; red first, where 2017 put blue first; and separate print and web values for the same six roles. `r g24_2017("color")`

### Qualitative palettes

The six-color order is **red, salmon, blue, light blue, dark gray, light gray**.
`economist_2024_pal(media)` returns it, and `scale_colour_economist_2024()` and `scale_fill_economist_2024()` use it.
The print colors are `r paste(unname(p24), collapse = ", ")`; the web colors are `r paste(unname(w24), collapse = ", ")`.

### Two reds: emphasis and single series

The published charts use two reds, and rarely in the same chart.
The deeper red of the palette above (`#ED1C24` in print, `#E3120B` on the web) marks emphasis: the first series of a chart with several, a highlighted bar, an interval, an annotation.
A brighter orange-red (`#F04F38` in print, `#F6423C` on the web) is the color of a plain single-series chart: one line, or a set of bars or columns all in one color.

| Measure | Print (94 charts) | Web, 2026 (118 charts) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Single-series red in a chart | 35 | 27 |
| Emphasis red in a chart, not counting the tab | 49 | about 80 |
| Both | 3 | 4 |

In print the single-series red is as common as salmon (35 charts against 36); on the web it is less common than salmon (27 against 43).
In both media it is more common than any blue or gray.
`economist_2024_pal()` returns it when asked for one color, so a discrete scale with one level, or `economist_2024_pal(media)(1)` for a single line, gets it; two or more colors start with the emphasis red.

### Evidence for separate web and print values

The distinction is visible in the exported assets, not inferred merely from the different backgrounds.
In the 118 web PNGs from 2026, exact `#E3120B` pixels occur in 108 graphics; salmon in 43, blue in 25, light blue in 15, dark gray in 10 and light gray in 22.
The six-series line chart `20260606_WOC055` contains all six web values as substantial runs of pixels.
The same values recur in the 308 Graphic Detail graphics of April 2024 to December 2025 (salmon in 144, blue in 64, light blue in 60, dark gray in 32, light gray in 50), so the web set has held since the redesign.
None of the six print values occurs in the web exports.
Conversely, `20260829_FNC090`, a print stacked-bar chart, contains all six print values and none of the six web values.
These are not two renditions of the same graphic, and, as the next section shows, the two sets are not conversions of each other either.

The print set is less secure than the web set beyond its first two colors.
Red and salmon recur throughout 2024--26, but `#28479D` blue appears in only five print charts, all from 2025--26, and `20260829_FNC090` is the one print chart with all six values.
In 2024 the print blues vary from chart to chart (`#3652A3`, `#222B76` and `#758FC0`, which is close to the web light blue).

### Print values are CMYK builds

The print colors are not the web colors converted for press.
Converting each web color to CMYK and back through a press profile (relative colorimetric with black-point compensation, the Adobe default) misses the print color by a median CIEDE2000 of 5.2 to 5.8 under each of U.S. Web Coated (SWOP) v2, Coated FOGRA39, Coated GRACoL 2006, Web Coated SWOP 2006 and Apple Generic CMYK: no closer than the web colors themselves.
The grays settle it. The web grays are warm and the print grays neutral, which no profile turns into each other.

Each print color is instead the rendering of a simple CMYK build through U.S. Web Coated (SWOP) v2, the profile the classic charts were exported through from 2015.
The red is 0/100/100/0, the brand guide's print spec for Economist Red, whose screen value is `#E3120B`; the same ink renders as `#ED1C24` through SWOP, which is why print and web reds differ.
The single-series red and salmon are tints of the same build along equal magenta and yellow, and the grays are black ink alone.
The web colors were chosen in RGB, from the design system's tokens.
The two sets share roles and order, not values.

```{r g24-print-cmyk, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  econ$print$palette[c("name", "cmyk", "hex", "observed", "delta_e", "confidence")],
  col.names = c("Color", "CMYK", "SWOP rendering", "Observed", "CIEDE2000", "Confidence"),
  align = "llllrl"
)
```

The specs are inferences: the simplest build (5% steps, 1% for the grounds) that reproduces each observed color.
Blue is less certain because the 2024 print blues varied, the grounds have several equally good fits, and no build reproduces the text color, which anti-aliasing blurs.
The table is `ggthemes_data$economist_2024$print$palette`; `data-raw/economist_2024_swop.R` reproduces it.

Only part of the chart palette is also an exact token in the current [Economist foundation palette](https://design-system.economist.com/foundations/colour/palettes):

| Role | Web chart value | Print chart value | Relation to foundation colors |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Red | `#E3120B` | `#ED1C24` | web is exactly Economist Red; print is its CMYK build |
| Salmon | `#FBA493` | `#F8AB90` | neither is an exact foundation token |
| Blue | `#3A4DAC` | `#28479D` | related to Chicago blue, but not an exact token |
| Light blue | `#7892C5` | `#659BD2` | related to Chicago blue, but not an exact token |
| Dark gray | `#6A6654` | `#636466` | the web gray is warm; the print gray is black ink alone |
| Light gray | `#BEBCAB` | `#C6C8CA` | the web gray is warm; the print gray is black ink alone |
| Ground | `#FFFFFF` | `#ECEBE0` | web is London 100; print is close to, but not, Los Angeles 90 `#EBE9E0` |

The web gray ramp does contain exact London gray tokens: `#F2F2F2`, `#D9D9D9`, `#B3B3B3` and `#0D0D0D`.
The chart blues clearly belong to the same visual family as Chicago blue, but treating them as official token values would overstate the evidence.

### Party colors

Political parties are the commonest case of color that means something outside the chart, and they take the palette where they can.
The left takes red and the right takes blue, so America's Republicans are red, against the usual American convention.
Second parties on each side take the paler partner: salmon for the Socialists & Democrats against the Left's red, and light blue for France's Republicans against the National Rally's blue.
In "Tanking", Trump's second term is red and his first salmon, and Biden is blue and Obama light blue, so the pairs are both party and recency.
Unaffiliated members and "others" take the palette's grays.

Only third parties go off the palette, and they take their own colors: amber for the liberal center (France's Ensemble, Renew Europe, Canada's New Democrats, Scotland's SNP), orange for Britain's Liberal Democrats, green for Greens, cyan for the European People's Party and Reform UK, and navy, dark red or dark green where a further party needs its own hue.
The values below are sampled from six charts of 2024–25 ("Tanking", "In poll position", "Squeezed middle", "Electoral efficiency", "Inching right" and "Not so separatist"). They match the print palette, not the web one.

| Color | Value | Parties |
|---|---|---|
| Red | `#ED1C24` | Trump (second term), Canada's Liberals, the European Left, Basque Socialists, Britain's Labour (as a line among many) |
| Single-series red | `#F04F38` | France's New Popular Front; Labour |
| Salmon | `#F8AB90` | Trump (first term), Socialists & Democrats |
| Blue | `#28479D` | Biden, Canada's Conservatives, National Rally, Britain's Conservatives, Spain's People's Party |
| Light blue | `#659BD2` to `#8AAFDC` | Obama, Bloc Québécois, France's Republicans, European Conservatives & Reformists |
| Dark gray | `#636466` | Unaffiliated (European Parliament) |
| Light gray | `#C6C8CA` | Others |
| Amber | `#FCB316` | Ensemble, Renew Europe, New Democrats, SNP (`#F9BE2A`) |
| Orange | `#F57F20` | Liberal Democrats |
| Green | `#71BF45` | Greens, EH Bildu; Plaid Cymru in a paler `#99CF87` |
| Cyan | `#2FC0D3` | European People's Party, Reform UK |
| Navy | `#222B76` | Identity & Democracy |
| Dark red | `#B7131A` | People's Party of Canada |
| Dark green | `#0A5115` | Basque Nationalist Party (PNV) |

The sampled values carry the antialiasing and compression of the images, so the off-palette ones are good to a few units.

### Sequential and diverging red and gray

Use red for a measure that carries the editorial focus and gray for neutral ordered context.
Both ramps run from light (low) to dark (high).
Use the diverging ramp only when the center has meaning: zero change, parity, a target or a long-run average.

These ramps are reconstructions, not sampled house ramps.
The web red ramp comes from one published map, `20260801_WOM946`.
The print gray steps lie on the blend between the text ink `#24211E` and the ground, so in the corpus they are mostly anti-aliased text; they are kept here as plausible warm-gray steps.
The web grays are exact London tokens of the design system.

```{r g24-gradients, econ_size = "two_column", econ_height = 150}
## One row per ramp, low to high, in each medium.
g24_ramps <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("print", "web"), function(media) {
  spec <- econ[[media]]
  rbind(
    data.frame(media = media, ramp = "Red", step = seq_len(nrow(spec$sequential_red)), hex = spec$sequential_red$value),
    data.frame(media = media, ramp = "Gray", step = seq_len(nrow(spec$sequential_gray)), hex = spec$sequential_gray$value),
    data.frame(media = media, ramp = "Red-gray", step = seq_len(nrow(spec$diverging)), hex = spec$diverging$value)
  )
}))
g24_ramps$row <- paste(g24_ramps$media, tolower(g24_ramps$ramp))
g24_ramps$row <- factor(g24_ramps$row, levels = rev(unique(g24_ramps$row)))

ggplot(g24_ramps, aes(step, row, fill = hex)) +
  geom_tile(width = 0.94, height = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = hex), size = g24_pt(3.6), colour = ifelse(g24_ramps$step > 3, "white", "black")) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0.01, 0)) +
  labs(title = "Sequential and diverging ramps", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  g24_theme("web") +
  g24_no_value_axis() +
  theme(axis.line = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_text(hjust = 0))
```

`scale_fill_gradient_economist_2024("red")` and `"gray"` use the sequential ramps, and `scale_fill_gradient2_economist_2024()` the diverging one; `guide_colourbar_economist_2024()` draws their key as the published charts do.

Against 2017: two ramps and one diverging scale, where the 2017 guide gave nine "equal lightness" scales, one for each of its hues. `r g24_2017("color")`

### Ordered categories

When the categories are ordered (generations, cohorts, age groups, classes), their colors run in the same order, and
the series the chart is about sits at one end of the run.
"He's got money, but not too much" (`20240420_EPC345`) draws seven birth cohorts across the life cycle, youngest
first: Gen Z is red, Millennials a deep salmon, Gen X the palette's salmon, and the four older cohorts take four
warm grays from light to dark, so that darker means older.
This is a ramp, not the six-color order, which is for categories that have none.
There is no key.
Each line is named beside itself in black, with its birth years under it, and only the focus, Gen Z, is in bold.
The names stand in the open, on gaps cut in the gridlines, and a name that has no room beside its line is joined to it
by a short black leader ending in a dot.

```{r g24-ordered-setup}
## Measured on `20240420_EPC345`, the print values: the red and salmon are the palette's; the deep salmon and the
## four warm grays are not (the lightest is not the palette's light gray `#C6C8CA`, which this chart keeps for its
## gridlines).
g24_ordered <- c(
  "Gen Z" = p24[["red"]], "Millennial" = "#E27A5E", "Gen X" = p24[["salmon"]], "Boomer" = "#C3C2B5",
  "Silent" = "#A4A495", "Greatest" = "#8A897D", "Lost" = "#64625D"
)
```

```{r g24-ordered-money, econ_height = 215}
## Approximate values read to follow the chart: median income by age, one value a year from each cohort's first age.
g24_cohort <- function(name, first, income) data.frame(cohort = name, age = first + seq_along(income) - 1, income = income)
g24_incomes <- rbind(
  g24_cohort("Gen Z", 15, c(36, 37.2, 38.2, 38.7, 38.5, 39, 39.3, 39.8, 40.1, 40.4, 41.1)),

                            43.8, 44.7, 45.4, 46.5, 47.7, 48.9, 49.6, 50.4, 50.7, 51.2, 50.1, 46.9)),

                               29, 29.1, 29.1, 29, 28.9, 28.7, 28.4, 27.9, 27.3, 26.6, 26.1, 25.9, 25.5, 25, 24.5, 24,

g24_incomes$cohort <- factor(g24_incomes$cohort, levels = names(g24_ordered))

## The names, set left-aligned with the birth years under them; the focus in bold. `at` is where each begins.
g24_cohort_names <- data.frame(
  label = c("Gen Z (born\n1997-2012)", "Millennial\n(1981-96)", "Gen X\n(1965-80)", "Boomer\n(1946-64)",
            "Silent\n(1928-45)", "Greatest\n(1901-27)", "Lost\n(1883-1900)"),
  x = c(13.2, 32.2, 58.1, 73.4, 13.2, 36.1, 70.3), y = c(45.2, 52.6, 52.6, 44.3, 12, 12.6, 8.9),
  face = c("bold", rep("plain", 6))
)
## Where a name stands on a gridline, the gridline stops.
g24_cohort_gaps <- data.frame(
  y = c(50, 50, 10, 10, 10), from = c(32, 54.6, 13.2, 35.8, 66.7), to = c(46.4, 67.4, 22.4, 50.2, 90)
)

g24_money <- ggplot(g24_incomes, aes(age, income, colour = cohort, group = cohort)) +
  ## Gridlines that stop where a name stands on them; the theme's own are switched off below.
  geom_gridline_economist_2024(seq(10, 50, 10), 13.1, 90, g24_cohort_gaps, base_size = g24_size) +
  geom_line(linewidth = g24_lw(1.5)) +
  ## Millennials' name has no room beside the end of their line: a leader runs down to it, ending in a dot.
  annotate("segment", x = 38.2, xend = 38.2, y = 49.6, yend = 45.5, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.1 * g24_size / ggplot2::.pt) +
  annotate("point", x = 38.2, y = 45.3, colour = "black", size = g24_pt(2.2)) +
  geom_text(data = g24_cohort_names, aes(x, y, label = label, fontface = face), colour = "black", hjust = 0,
            lineheight = 0.95, size = g24_text, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = g24_ordered, guide = "none") +
  g24_value_axis(limits = c(0, 55.8), breaks = seq(0, 50, 10), expand = c(0, 0), oob = scales::oob_keep) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(13.1, 90), expand = c(0, 0), breaks = c(15, seq(20, 80, 10), 89)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "He’s got money, but not too much",
    subtitle = "United States, median income after\ntaxes and transfers*, $’000, 2019 prices",
    x = "Age, years", y = NULL, caption = "Source: Federal Reserve\nworking paper"
  ) +
  g24_theme() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), axis.title.x = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

g24_chart(g24_money, footnote = "*Adjusted by\nhousehold size", number = 4)
```

Against 2017: the 2017 guide's ordered colors were nine "equal lightness" scales, one for each hue, with no focus in them; here the focus is the red end of a red-salmon-gray run, so the ramp both orders the series and picks out the one the story is about.
`r g24_2017("color")`

## Production recipe

```{r g24-production-recipe, eval = FALSE}
p <- ggplot(data, aes(date, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = economist_2024_pal("print")(1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(guide = guide_axis_economist_2017(), position = "right") +
  labs(
    title = "A short headline",
    subtitle = "Geography, measure, unit and period",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "*Note, if any\nSource: Organisation or dataset"
  ) +
  theme_economist_2024(media = "print", base_family = "Economist Sans")

economist_2024_chart(p, "print")
```

Before export, check:

- Does the headline name what matters?
- Are geography, unit, period and denominator present?
- Is this the simplest chart type that answers the question?
- Does red identify the intended focus?
- Are series labelled directly where practical?
- Do bars start at zero?
- Are uncertainty, forecasts and omitted periods explicit?
- Do headline, plot and source share a left edge?
- Has web output been checked at 700px, 550px and the mobile width?

## Method and limitations

The local corpus contains issue-organized print PNGs from 2012--2026 and web graphics from 2024--2026.
Exact colors were counted from the indexed PNG color tables.
Original `ai2html` files supplied type families, CSS weights, sizes, line heights and responsive artboard widths.

The print sample is uneven: 94 print charts from after the redesign (39 from 2024, 26 from 2025 and 29 from a single 2026 issue).
Print images after April 2024 are not in the web archive, so the 2025 and 2026 charts were collected one by one and later print coverage is thin.
The layout counts in this guide come from a chart-by-chart survey of 88 of the 94 print charts and all 118 web graphics of 2026.
The web sample is larger: 118 graphics from 2026, with their `ai2html` sources, and 308 Graphic Detail graphics from April 2024 to December 2025.
This is enough to establish the ground, qualitative order and recurring grammar, but not to turn every rare layout into a rule.
The examples added later (ribbons, rank charts, highlighted scatters, log scales, dotted forecasts and tables with boxed figures) come from print charts of 2024 and 2025 outside the survey, found while the full 2024-onward print archive was still being collected; the survey's counts were not redone for them.
Where a 2017 chart type does not appear in the corpus, its 2024 version here applies the general rules, and says so.
